source_acquisition.search_note: PDF metadata and reading identify the authors’ project URL https://sites.google.com/view/pcd-iclr26, GitHub repository https://github.com/jatan12/PCD, and the official proceedings PDF. The inventory row marks jatan12/PCD as exact_visual_source and lists the acquired plot/table family. GitHub metadata matched the paper title and describes the repository as the ICLR 2026 official implementation; default branch master was inspected at commit 663ae3e41f34483175a6c6b581d870eff88d4a04. The local source set contains plot helpers and scripts/produce_tables.py, but not the paper TeX or an explicit Figure 1/2 diagram assembly. Therefore all visual properties are labelled rendered_estimate or mixed unless a source file states the parameter directly; the PDF remains the fact source for object count, layout, labels, and captions. Inventory-only notebooks, rendered benchmark PDFs, and unrelated plotting helpers were not treated as object-specific source files without a local acquisition path.

paper_style.palette_strategy: 结果折线图使用低饱和 categorical task palette，以 marker 形状提供部分冗余；概念图用淡蓝/淡黄阶段底色与蓝/橙角色色；散点图用角色或 non-dominated front 的颜色。颜色来自 PDF 渲染估计，公开源则明确使用 Times New Roman、linewidth 1.5、YlGnBu 或 red/green/pink/blue 角色色。
paper_style.vector_raster_mix: PDF 33 页由可缩放文字、路径和表格规则为主，图表页未整页栅格化；概念管线和散点/折线/直方图可在 200 dpi PNG 中检查。源仓库还保存 PNG/PDF 导出路径，但本审计不把这些辅助资产当作 PDF 对象清单。
paper_style.style_consistency: 正文 caption 与表格保持 Nimbus Roman/Computer Modern 数学字体外观，图内坐标文字呈 DejaVu Sans/Times New Roman 家族混合。结果图的线宽、网格和 marker 系统较稳定；附录长表统一 booktabs、无竖线，但字号显著压缩。

figures.label: Figure 1

caption.text: Figure 1: Overview of the PCD framework, which reframes offline MOO as a conditional sampling problem. Training: A conditional diffusion model is trained on a static dataset, using a novel reweighting strategy to emphasize high-quality solutions near the Pareto front. Sampling: At inference, the model directly generates novel designs conditioned on target objectives. This end-to-end approach sidesteps the need for the explicit surrogate models and separate optimizers required by prior methods.

color.semantic_mapping: Blue blocks identify the diffusion model; orange/yellow accents mark data, target objectives, and sampling; pale backgrounds separate the two stages.

encodings.y: two horizontal lanes, with model and data roles aligned across lanes
encodings.color: pale blue and yellow stage backgrounds, blue model blocks, orange data/condition roles
encodings.shape: rounded containers, model boxes, data/noise icons, and arrowheads
encodings.line: solid process arrows and dashed lane boundaries
encodings.text: stage titles, dataset/model labels, Noise, Condition, Sample, and Designs

figures.data_and_statistics: Conceptual interface only. The diagram names a static dataset, reweighting, target objectives, and generated designs but reports no sample count, objective units, model score, aggregation, or uncertainty.
figures.evidence_relation: Introduction tension between offline extrapolation and reliability → Figure 1 pipeline → Section 4 reweighting and reference directions → Tables 1–2 and Figures 3–9 test performance and mechanisms.
design_strengths: The shared model block visually connects training and sampling without introducing a separate surrogate.
Dashed containers and directional arrows give the claimed end-to-end process a recoverable causal order.
The caption states the conceptual claim and the alternative pipeline it replaces.
design_weaknesses: Small labels and decorative icons compete with the two key transitions at page scale.
Color carries stage and object roles, so the distinction weakens in grayscale even though position and text provide partial redundancy.
The diagram does not expose the conditioning-point generation detail that Figure 2 later supplies.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use a two-lane full-width pipeline to contrast offline training with target-conditioned inference while keeping the model interface visually identical.

evidence.label: p.2 Figure 1 rendered object and caption

figures.label: Figure 2

caption.text: Figure 2: Overview of the conditioning points generation procedure: a) The objective space is partitioned via direction vectors, and points are ranked based on non-dominated sorting. b) Each direction vector is paired with the point closest to it in perpendicular distance (black arrow). The rest of the points are paired to the vector with the least amount of assigned points (gray arrow). c) A diverse set of conditioning points is generated by extrapolating the assigned points along the direction vectors and adding Gaussian noise.

color.semantic_mapping: Point colours distinguish ranked or newly generated roles; black and gray arrows encode two assignment rules and provide non-colour redundancy.

encodings.shape: points, direction vectors, arrows, and noisy extrapolated points
encodings.line: direction rays plus black nearest and gray load-balancing arrows
encodings.facet: a partition/rank, b assignment, c extrapolation/noise
encodings.text: panel labels, objective axes, direction labels, and point-role annotations

figures.data_and_statistics: Geometric mechanism illustration. It encodes no measured outcome, repeated-run statistic, or uncertainty; the points and vectors are schematic examples of the reference-direction procedure.
figures.evidence_relation: Section 4 reference-direction procedure → Figure 2 construction → Algorithm 2 on p.24 → Table 2 and Table 7 ablations of conditioning and direction generation.
design_strengths: The three steps expose a mechanism that would be opaque in a formula alone.
Black and gray arrow semantics are explicitly defined in the caption and visually aligned with the assignment operations.
Shared axes make the progression from ranking to noisy extrapolation easy to follow.
design_weaknesses: The schematic points are not labelled with cardinality or a concrete dataset, so readers cannot infer scale.
Several pastel point groups and arrows require the caption for role decoding; grayscale separation is limited.
The final noise operation is represented symbolically rather than showing the distribution parameters later listed in Table 3.
figures.reusable_pattern: Turn a reference-direction algorithm into three aligned objective-space snapshots: rank, assign, then extrapolate and perturb.

evidence.label: p.5 Figure 2 rendered object and caption

figures.label: Figure 3

caption.text: Figure 3: Effect of the guidance scale γ on the normalized HV ratio across five representative tasks. Performance saturates quickly, showing limited benefit from strong guidance.

color.semantic_mapping: Each colour identifies one task; distinct marker shapes provide a second task cue.

encodings.x: guidance scale γ at five discrete settings
encodings.y: normalized HV ratio relative to default γ = 2.5
encodings.line: one line per task connecting guidance settings
encodings.text: axis labels, tick values, legend entries, and γ notation

figures.data_and_statistics: Each mark is a normalized hypervolume ratio for one representative task and guidance setting; the curve is not an uncertainty summary and no error bars or bands are shown. The normalization reference is γ = 2.5, stated in the surrounding text rather than the caption.
figures.evidence_relation: Section 5.4 guidance-scale ablation → Figure 3 tests classifier-free guidance strength → Table 3 records the default γ = 2.5 → broader HV comparisons in Table 1 and Appendix Tables 9–32.
design_strengths: A common ratio scale makes quick saturation visible across tasks.
Five marker shapes and a legend preserve task identity beyond line colour.
The caption states the practical ablation conclusion rather than merely naming the parameter.
design_weaknesses: Discrete, non-uniform γ settings are displayed as a categorical sequence, which can be mistaken for a continuous response curve.
The caption omits the normalization baseline and uncertainty convention, so exact variability requires the surrounding text or source data.
Five lines converge near one and become difficult to distinguish at the default setting.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use a shared normalized baseline and marker-coded task lines for a compact guidance or sampling hyperparameter sweep.

evidence.label: p.10 Figure 3 rendered object and caption

figures.label: Figure 4

caption.text: Figure 4: Normalized dominance number distributions reveal dataset quality differences. The narrow distributions of C10/MOP2 and MO-Hopper indicate consistently high-quality datasets, whereas the long-tailed distribution of ZDT2 signals high variance in sample quality.

color.semantic_mapping: One muted teal/green distribution fill identifies each task panel; task titles provide the primary redundant cue.

encodings.text: panel task titles and shared axis labels

figures.data_and_statistics: Distributional diagnostic of sample quality. Histogram heights are density values; the figure does not report the sample count, bin-width rule, numerical moments, or uncertainty intervals.
figures.evidence_relation: Section A.1 links dominance-number spread to reweighting → Figure 4 motivates temperature sensitivity in Figure 5 → Table 2 tests reweighting against pruning and no processing.
design_strengths: Small multiples align three dataset-quality regimes on one page.
The long-tail versus concentrated-shape contrast communicates the mechanism without an additional legend.
Panel titles and shared axes reduce repeated annotation.
design_weaknesses: Different y-axis ranges make visual bar height comparisons across tasks unsafe without reading ticks.
The density and binning choices are not defined in the caption.
A single fill colour per panel carries little redundant encoding if the panel title is overlooked.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use matched histogram panels to diagnose data-quality heterogeneity before interpreting a reweighting sweep.

evidence.label: p.16 Figure 4 rendered object and caption

figures.label: Figure 5

caption.text: Figure 5: Effect of the reweighting temperature τ on normalized performance. For the high-variance ZDT2 dataset, increasing τ significantly improves performance. The effect is minimal on the low-variance datasets.

color.semantic_mapping: Tan identifies ZDT2, pink C10/MOP2, and blue MO-Hopper-v2; marker shape repeats the task identity.

encodings.y: normalized performance relative to default τ = 0.05
encodings.text: axis labels, task legend, and τ symbol

figures.data_and_statistics: Each point is a normalized hypervolume result at one temperature for ZDT2, C10/MOP2, or MO-Hopper-v2; no uncertainty bars or bands are displayed. The default normalization τ = 0.05 is explained in the surrounding appendix text, not the caption.
figures.evidence_relation: Figure 4 data-quality diagnosis → Figure 5 tests whether temperature should soften reweighting on long-tailed data → Table 3 fixes τ = 0.05 as the default and Table 2 tests the full reweighting component.
design_strengths: The same normalized ratio language as Figure 3 makes the two sensitivity plots comparable.
The ZDT2 trajectory separates from the two flatter task trajectories, directly supporting the caption finding.
The compact legend leaves the right side of the chart open for the rising curve.
design_weaknesses: The legend overlays plot area and can obscure low-temperature points.
The caption does not define the denominator or report replicate variability.
The numeric τ positions are sparse, so connecting lines imply interpolation between widely separated settings.
figures.reusable_pattern: Keep the baseline temperature visible on a shared normalized y-scale, and use small multiples only when task-specific trajectories need comparison.

evidence.label: p.17 Figure 5 rendered object and caption

figures.label: Figure 6

caption.text: Figure 6: Impact of noise scale and extrapolation distance on conditioning point generation. Left: Increasing the noise scale has a limited, yet positive impact on performance. Right: Increasing the extrapolation distance leads to diminishing returns.

color.semantic_mapping: Pink, blue, and orange identify C10/MOP2, MO-Hopper-v2, and RE23; marker shapes repeat the mapping.

encodings.x: noise scale σ or extrapolation distance, depending on panel
encodings.color: task identity shared across both panels
encodings.line: connecting lines with vertical error bars
encodings.facet: noise scale left; extrapolation distance right
encodings.text: panel headers, x-axis labels, shared y-axis label, legend, and σ

figures.data_and_statistics: Point estimates are normalized hypervolume ratios for C10/MOP2, MO-Hopper-v2, and RE23. Vertical error bars show run-to-run variation, but the caption does not define whether they are SD, SE, or a confidence interval; no band or sample count is shown.
figures.evidence_relation: Section A.6 introduces sampling hyperparameter ablations → Figure 6 tests diversity noise and extrapolation distance → Table 3 records default values → Figure 8 explains why distant conditioning can fail on MO-Hopper.
design_strengths: Shared y-scale and legend make the two parameter effects comparable.
Error bars keep the visible variance aligned with the appendix discussion of extrapolation uncertainty.
Panel titles and distinct x variables prevent the two sweeps from being read as one parameter.
design_weaknesses: The x-axis combines two different parameter domains in one wide coordinate system, so each panel must be read independently.
The caption omits the statistic represented by error bars and the number of runs.
Several series overlap near the baseline and rely on marker colour/shape for separation.
figures.reusable_pattern: Pair adjacent parameter sweeps with a shared y-axis, shared legend, and explicit error-bar semantics.

evidence.label: p.20 Figure 6 rendered object and caption

figures.label: Figure 7

caption.text: Figure 7: Hypervolume ratio as a function of denoising steps. Performance remains consistent across increasing numbers of steps for most tasks, demonstrating that PCD generates high-quality solutions efficiently even with fewer sampling steps.

color.semantic_mapping: Pink, blue, orange, green, and tan map to the five benchmark tasks; marker shapes repeat the mapping.

encodings.x: number of denoising steps at six discrete budgets
encodings.line: task trajectories with vertical error bars
encodings.text: axis labels, task legend, and denoising-step ticks

figures.data_and_statistics: Point estimates compare hypervolume ratios at discrete denoising budgets for five tasks; error bars encode visible variability but their statistic is not defined in the caption. The plot contains no explicit time-per-sample measurement, so efficiency is inferred from maintaining quality with fewer steps.
figures.evidence_relation: Section A.6.4 asks whether the 1024-step default is necessary → Figure 7 supplies the quality-versus-step evidence → Table 3 records 1024 default steps → Table 4 reports wall-clock sampling cost.
design_strengths: The discrete budget sweep directly answers whether extra diffusion steps change quality.
A shared legend and marker system carries task identities through overlap.
The caption links flat performance to a practical fewer-step conclusion.
design_weaknesses: The x values are discrete but connected with lines, which suggests continuous interpolation.
The Regex error bars are much larger and can dominate the visual scale without a caption definition.
Quality ratio alone does not quantify actual latency reduction.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use a discrete compute-budget sweep with uncertainty bars and a normalized quality metric, then pair it with an explicit wall-clock table.

evidence.label: p.21 Figure 7 rendered object and caption

figures.label: Figure 8

caption.text: Figure 8: Qualitative analysis of Pareto-conditioning effectiveness. Left (MO-Hopper): On this high-dimensional task, the model struggles to generate solutions that improve upon the first objective. Right (RE21): On this lower-dimensional task, the conditioning is highly effective: the generated points (y_out) closely align with and even outperform their conditioning targets (ŷ).

color.semantic_mapping: Blue circles identify D(best), green diamonds y_out, and pink triangles ŷ; shape and legend provide redundancy.

encodings.color: role of D(best), y_out, or ŷ
encodings.shape: circle, diamond, and triangle role markers
encodings.text: panel task titles, axis labels, legend, and y_out/ŷ notation

figures.data_and_statistics: Qualitative objective-space comparison. Each point is an objective vector from the best offline set, generated conditioning set, or generated outcome; no uncertainty, aggregation, front membership, or count is encoded.
figures.evidence_relation: Section A.7 case study → Figure 8 tests whether conditioned outputs follow or exceed target objectives → Figure 9 tests reconstruction from original data points → Table 16 and Table 12 provide corresponding MORL and RE21 numeric context.
design_strengths: Marker shape cleanly separates target, source-best, and generated outcome roles.
The contrasting task panels make the high-dimensional failure and lower-dimensional success visible without a dense quantitative legend.
The caption states the directional interpretation of alignment and improvement.
design_weaknesses: A common marker palette across panels does not show which points belong to a Pareto front or replicate.
The left legend sits over the plot and can cover points.
The high-dimensional task is represented through a two-coordinate projection without stating the projection or objective scaling.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use role-coded scatter markers in paired easy-versus-hard panels to connect a mechanism claim to an interpretable qualitative failure case.

evidence.label: p.21 Figure 8 rendered object and caption

figures.label: Figure 9

caption.text: Figure 9: Analysis of the model’s ability to reconstruct the original data distribution. Colors represent distinct non-dominated fronts (F_i) extracted from the training set. The model is conditioned on the objective vectors of the original data (circles, ŷ); successful reconstruction is achieved if the generated solutions (crosses, y_out) overlap with these circles. Left (MO-Hopper): In this high-dimensional task, the model is unable to capture the original data distribution it was trained on. Right (RE21): In this simpler task, the model faithfully reconstructs the original conditioning points.

color.semantic_mapping: Front identity uses multiple categorical colours; gray legend samples and marker shapes identify conditioning circles versus outcome crosses.

encodings.shape: circle for conditioning point and cross for generated outcome
encodings.text: panel task titles, axis labels, legend, F_i notation, and y_out/ŷ labels

figures.data_and_statistics: Qualitative reconstruction test. Colours identify fronts and markers identify original versus generated vectors; the plot has no point counts, matching criterion, uncertainty, or distance statistic.
figures.evidence_relation: Figure 8’s target/outcome case study → Figure 9 isolates in-distribution reconstruction → Appendix A.7 discussion bounds PCD’s high-dimensional generalization claim and complements Tables 12/16.
design_strengths: Front colours preserve the internal structure of the source dataset rather than collapsing all points into one cloud.
Circle/cross marker redundancy makes the reconstruction criterion visible without relying only on colour.
The paired task choice turns a broad reconstruction claim into a direct contrast.
design_weaknesses: Many overlapping points and front colours create high local density, particularly in MO-Hopper.
The legend defines roles but not the number or ordering of fronts; colour decoding is weak in grayscale.
Overlap is judged visually without a quantitative reconstruction distance or success threshold.
figures.reusable_pattern: Overlay source and generated objective vectors with front colour and role marker redundancy when a generative model must demonstrate distribution reconstruction.

evidence.label: p.22 Figure 9 rendered object and caption

tables.label: Table 1

caption.text: Table 1: Average rank (↓) of PCD and baseline methods across five task categories. Ranks are calculated based on the 100th percentile HV. Bold and underlined rows indicate the best and runner up methods respectively. PCD achieves the best overall average rank, demonstrating its strong and consistent performance.

tables.uncertainty: mean±SD appears for each category and Avg. rank; D(best) is a dataset reference row without a separate sampling uncertainty definition.
tables.data_and_statistics: Average rank over Synthetic, MORL, RE, Scientific, and MONAS plus an overall rank; lower is better and values are reported to two decimals.
tables.evidence_relation: Results in §5.3 use Table 1 to support the consistency claim; Appendix Tables 9–16 provide 100th-percentile per-task HV details, with Tables 17–32 giving lower percentiles.
design_strengths: The category headers compress five benchmark families plus the aggregate into one decision row.
Bold and underline create a direct best-versus-runner-up cue without cell colouring.
design_weaknesses: The 15-method body is dense and abbreviations require the method discussion.
Rank aggregation hides per-task scale and the caption does not define how ties or category weighting enter the average.
tables.reusable_pattern: Use a compact rank summary as a bridge from many per-task appendix tables to one headline consistency claim.

evidence.label: p.8 Table 1 rendered object and caption

tables.label: Table 2

caption.text: Table 2: Average 100th percentile HV (↑) on 5 representative tasks with different data processing and sampling strategies. Bold and underlined rows indicate the best and runner up methods respectively. The results validate the effectiveness of both our proposed reweighting and reference-direction mechanisms.

tables.uncertainty: Each cell is an average 100th-percentile HV with a ± spread over runs; the caption does not name SD or SE.
tables.data_and_statistics: Five ablation variants cross five representative tasks; HV is the reported metric and the table compares Ideal, D(best), Ref. Dir., pruning, and full PCD.
tables.evidence_relation: The §5.4 ablation text calls Table 2 the evidence for reweighting and reference-direction components; Table 3 supplies defaults and Figures 3–7 probe adjacent choices.
design_strengths: The Variant column makes the component combination readable before the task columns.
Best and runner-up emphasis makes the full PCD row easy to locate.
design_weaknesses: Only five tasks represent the broader benchmark; the metric’s units and reference point are not restated.
Variant labels mix sampling and data-processing factors, so the factorial structure must be inferred from the prose.
tables.reusable_pattern: Cross component variants in rows and representative tasks in columns, then point to full per-task tables for coverage.

evidence.label: p.9 Table 2 rendered object and caption

tables.label: Table 3

caption.text: Table 3: Default hyperparameters for PCD framework including Residual MLP Denoiser for reweighted training (left) and EDM Sampling (right). If multiple values were used, bolded value indicates default value.

tables.uncertainty: No repeated-run uncertainty; this is a configuration table. Multiple candidate values are listed in the CFG Guidance Scale row, with the default bolded.
tables.data_and_statistics: Two parallel Parameter/Value(s) blocks cover the Residual MLP Denoiser and EDM sampler, including reweighting, query budget, directions, and CFG defaults.
tables.evidence_relation: Appendix A.3 makes Table 3 the reproducibility anchor for Figure 3 guidance, Figures 5–7 sensitivity, Algorithm 1, and the main experiments.
design_strengths: The two-block header exposes training and sampling defaults without duplicating a long table.
Bold default selection preserves the distinction between a sweep and the fixed configuration.
design_weaknesses: Small math symbols and mixed units make rows such as σmin, Snoise, and CFG Guidance Scale slower to scan.
A central divider is the only strong group separator, while the caption does not define every acronym.
tables.reusable_pattern: Present coupled training and sampler configuration in parallel blocks with one explicit default marker.

evidence.label: p.17 Table 3 rendered object and caption

tables.label: Table 4

caption.text: Table 4: Computational cost comparison. We report the one-time dataset reweighting cost (seconds) and sampling times (seconds) averaged over 3 runs. PCD demonstrates faster sampling speeds compared to the generative baseline ParetoFlow across four representative tasks, while reweighting adds negligible overhead.

tables.uncertainty: Reweighting and sampling times are averages over three runs and use ± spreads; dataset counts and dimensions are deterministic. The caption specifies seconds but not the spread statistic.
tables.data_and_statistics: A Method column spans two row groups: Dataset Info with samples/objectives/dimensions/reweighting time, then Sampling Time with PCD and ParetoFlow seconds across four tasks.
tables.evidence_relation: Appendix A.4 connects Table 4 to the quadratic dominance-number preprocessing claim, Figure 7’s fewer-step efficiency interpretation, and the main PCD/ParetoFlow comparison.
design_strengths: Grouped row headers separate one-time preprocessing from repeated sampling cost.
The same task columns support cost comparisons without losing dataset scale context.
design_weaknesses: Mixed row units force the reader to switch between counts, dimensions, and seconds.
The caption does not report hardware in the table, although hardware is only described in surrounding prose.
tables.reusable_pattern: Place dataset scale, preprocessing cost, and sampling cost in one grouped table when runtime claims depend on problem size.

evidence.label: p.18 Table 4 rendered object and caption

tables.label: Table 5

caption.text: Table 5: Average 100th percentile HV (↑) on 5 different tasks comparing EDM with stochastic and deterministic samplers. Bold and underlined rows indicate the best and runner up methods respectively. The default stochastic sampler shows superior performance on most tasks.

tables.uncertainty: Cells report mean±spread for five task HV values; the caption does not define the spread as SD or SE.
tables.data_and_statistics: Four sampler/reweighting variants are compared across C10/MOP2, MO-Hopper-v2, RE34, Regex, and ZDT2 at the 100th percentile.
tables.evidence_relation: Appendix A.5 uses Table 5 to justify stochastic EDM as default, and Table 3 records the resulting sampler configuration.
design_strengths: Rows isolate stochastic versus deterministic sampling and the effect of removing reweighting.
Task columns expose the Regex exception that the prose discusses.
design_weaknesses: The long method labels are visually heavy relative to narrow task columns.
No explicit sample count or error-statistic definition appears in the caption.
tables.reusable_pattern: Make sampler choice falsifiable by pairing stochastic/deterministic rows with the same task columns and retaining the component control rows.

evidence.label: p.19 Table 5 rendered object and caption

tables.label: Table 6

caption.text: Table 6: Average 100th percentile Hypervolume (↑) on 5 different tasks using varying numbers of conditioning points J. Bold and underlined rows indicate the best and runner up methods respectively. Increasing the number of selected points generally yields higher performance, with J = 32 achieving the best results on the majority of tasks.

tables.uncertainty: Cells report mean±spread of 100th-percentile HV over five tasks; the spread statistic and run count are not stated in the caption.
tables.data_and_statistics: Five conditioning-point counts J = 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 form the rows, with tasks C10/MOP2, MO-Hopper-v2, RE34, Regex, and ZDT2 as columns.
tables.evidence_relation: Appendix A.6.1 uses Table 6 to establish the default J = 32 used in Table 3 and to contextualize the target-generation mechanism in Figure 2.
design_strengths: The monotone J row sequence makes the default and exception easy to scan.
Bold/underline highlighting focuses attention on per-task best values rather than only one aggregate.
design_weaknesses: The caption’s “generally” finding has a Regex exception that readers must inspect cell by cell.
J notation and task abbreviations are not expanded in the table.
tables.reusable_pattern: Use ordered hyperparameter rows and aligned task columns to expose both a general trend and task-specific exceptions.

evidence.label: p.19 Table 6 rendered object and caption

tables.label: Table 7

caption.text: Table 7: Average 100th percentile HV (↑) comparing Riesz s-Energy (default) and Das-Dennis methods for generating direction vectors. Bold rows indicate the best method. The simpler Das-Dennis method yields slightly better results, though the difference is minimal, indicating robustness.

tables.uncertainty: Cells report mean±spread of 100th-percentile HV for two direction-vector methods; no uncertainty convention is defined in the caption.
tables.data_and_statistics: Two method rows compare Riesz s-Energy and Das-Dennis across five representative tasks; bold marks the better cell.
tables.evidence_relation: Appendix A.6.3 ties Table 7 to Figure 2’s direction-vector mechanism and the robustness claim that the generation choice has marginal effect.
design_strengths: The two-row layout makes the method substitution transparent.
The caption reports the practical trade-off between tunability and simplicity.
design_weaknesses: Bold-only emphasis does not show how small the differences are without reading values.
The method names and capitalization vary between caption and body.
tables.reusable_pattern: Use a two-row replacement table when testing whether a geometric construction is robust to its generator.

evidence.label: p.20 Table 7 rendered object and caption

tables.label: Table 8

caption.text: Table 8: Scalability analysis on many-objective DTLZ tasks. We report the relative Hypervolume improvement (↑) of PCD over the best offline dataset solutions (D(best)). PCD achieves consistent performance improvements regardless of the number of objectives (m).

tables.uncertainty: Relative HV improvement values are reported without ± uncertainty; the table is a deterministic scalability slice.
tables.data_and_statistics: Rows are DTLZ1 and DTLZ7; grouped columns report relative improvement for m = 3, 4, 5, and 6 objectives.
tables.evidence_relation: Appendix A.8 extends the two-objective evidence to many-objective settings and complements the MORL/DTLZ rows in the large result tables.
design_strengths: The grouped objective-count header makes scalability dimension explicit.
Relative improvement normalizes away raw dataset quality and objective scale as described in the surrounding text.
design_weaknesses: Only two synthetic functions are shown, so the scalability claim is narrower than the caption wording.
No baseline or absolute HV context is embedded in the table.
tables.reusable_pattern: Add a grouped objective-count header when a method’s claim depends on scaling the number of objectives.

evidence.label: p.23 Table 8 rendered object and caption

cross_object_system.visual_narrative: Figure 1 先把 offline MOO 重述为 conditional sampling；Figure 2 给出 reference-direction conditioning mechanism；Table 1 是跨五类任务的 headline rank，Table 2 是组件消融，Figure 3–7 依次覆盖 guidance、dataset quality/reweighting、noise/extrapolation、denoising budget；Figures 8–9 以 MO-Hopper 与 RE21 的定性 failure/reconstruction 收束，Tables 9–32 提供三个 percentile 的逐任务底表。
cross_object_system.caption_system: Figure captions 使用 “Figure n:” 加标题、设置和结论，主结果与敏感性图通常直接陈述发现；Figure 2 偏机制说明，Figure 8/9 明确定义 marker 角色。Table 1–8 的 caption 说明指标、方向、比较和高亮，Table 9–32 仅给出 percentile/domain 标题，统计 spread、任务定义和 N/A 语义留给正文或表体。
cross_object_system.table_header_system: 主结果和消融表采用 Method/Variant 加任务列的单层表头；Table 3 用两组 Parameter/Value(s) 并列训练与 EDM，Table 4 用 Dataset Info/Sampling Time 行组，Table 8 用 No. objectives 的二层列组。长附录表保持 Method-first、任务横向、三种 percentile 分卷。
cross_object_system.method_result_ablation_link: Figure 1/2 是方法接口与机制；Table 2、Figure 3、Figure 5–7 和 Tables 5–7 将 reweighting、CFG、noise、J、direction vectors、sampler 与 denoising steps 逐一拆解；Table 1 和 Tables 9–32 负责综合比较；Figures 8–9 解释 MORL/RE21 的定性成功与失败边界。
cross_object_system.main_appendix_link: 正文 Figure 1–3 与 Tables 1–2 形成主论证；Appendix A.1–A.8 的 Figures 4–9 和 Tables 3–8 回接每个设计选择；Appendix A.11–A.13 Tables 9–32 由 §5.3 的 Table 1 调用，作为 100/75/50 percentile 的逐任务可复核底表。Algorithm 1 和 Algorithm 2 也已逐页检查，但因 schema 仅建模 Figure/Table，未放入 figures/tables 数组。
cross_object_system.typography_consistency: 正文和 captions 的 serif 字体与数学符号统一，图内 axes 使用 sans/Times New Roman 风格；表格 body/header 约 6.4–8 pt，长表在 200 dpi 仍可读但不适合快速比较。
cross_object_system.color_consistency: task-series 折线跨 Figure 3、5、6、7 复用 marker/颜色语义但任务集合不同；散点图在 Figure 8 以角色色，在 Figure 9 以 front 色，导致跨图颜色不可作全局语义。所有颜色在 grayscale 下均需结合 marker、面板标题或文字。

most_reusable_patterns: 用全宽 Offline Training/Sampling 双 lane 固定数据、模型、条件与生成结果的接口。
用三步 objective-space small multiple 把 reference-direction 算法变成可检查的 rank → assign → extrapolate/noise 视觉语法。
用统一 normalized HV ratio、task marker 和 shared legend 组织 guidance、temperature、noise、distance、denoising-step 的敏感性图，并用 booktabs 长表保留逐任务底表。
highest_value_objects: Figure 1：把离线 MOO 的方法主张压缩成训练与采样两段端到端接口。
Figure 2：解释 conditioning points 生成机制，是 Table 2/7 消融的视觉前提。
Table 1：跨五类任务给出一致性 headline，且可回链 Tables 9–32。
Figure 8/9：将高维 MO-Hopper 的 failure 与 RE21 的 reconstruction success 具体化。
failure_patterns: Figure 3、5、7 把离散超参数点用折线连接，但 caption 没有完整说明归一化基准、spread 或数据分母。
Figure 6/7 的 error bars 未在 caption 中定义 SD/SE 或重复次数；Figure 8/9 的点云没有 count、distance 或匹配阈值。
Tables 9–32 以极小字号承载 15×多任务矩阵，caption 缺少任务定义、spread、N/A 和 percentile 解释，适合查表而非独立阅读。
公开仓库提供 plot/table 家族和 exact defaults，但没有论文 TeX 或 Figure 1/2 的明确组装源；必须以 PDF 的对象布局与 caption 为事实源。
final_judgment.one_sentence_visual_strategy: 先用全宽 pipeline 和三步几何图解释 PCD 的 conditional sampling 与 reference-direction mechanism，再用 normalized-HV 敏感性/消融、headline rank 和逐任务 percentile 表验证效果，并以 MO-Hopper/RE21 的定性对照暴露泛化边界。
